kernel.sched_cfs_bandwidth_slice_us.desc: 1. When finer control over CFS bandwidth allocation is needed (e.g., in high-load container environments), this value (default 5000 microseconds) can be appropriately decreased, but note that excessively small values will increase scheduling overhead; 2. In scenarios where CPU resources are sufficient and the goal is to reduce scheduling overhead, this value can be increased to decrease the allocation frequency from the global time pool

kernel.sched_latency_ns.desc: 1. When the system runs high-priority real-time tasks and experiences high scheduling latency, this value can be appropriately decreased to improve scheduling response speed; 2. For systems with CPU-intensive workloads and a large number of tasks (exceeding 8 logical CPUs), this value should be increased to reduce context switching overhead

kernel.sched_min_granularity_ns.desc: 1. When the system load is high and there are many short-running processes, this value can be appropriately increased to reduce context switching overhead. It is recommended to gradually increase it from the default value (usually 1,000,000 ns) and test, observing performance changes; 2. For CPU-intensive workloads where processes generally have long runtimes, this value can be appropriately decreased to improve system responsiveness. It is recommended to gradually decrease it from the default value and test

transparent_hugepage.defrag.desc: 1. For applications requiring low latency (e.g., databases, real-time systems), it is recommended to disable this parameter (set to 'never') to avoid performance fluctuations caused by memory defragmentation; 2. For memory-intensive applications that are not latency-sensitive (e.g., batch processing jobs), it is recommended to enable this parameter (set to 'always' or 'defer+madvise') to increase large memory page usage and reduce TLB misses

transparent_hugepage.enabled.desc: 1. For latency-sensitive applications (e.g., databases, real-time systems), it is recommended to disable it (set to 'never' or 'madvise') to avoid unpredictable latency caused by transparent huge page defragmentation; 2. For memory-intensive batch processing jobs (e.g., scientific computing, big data processing), it is recommended to enable it (set to 'always') to improve memory access efficiency by reducing page table entries

net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max.desc: 1. When the server handles a large number of concurrent connections (e.g., exceeding the default value of 65536) and kernel logs show 'table full' related messages or frequent connection tracking table full conditions leading to packet loss, this value should be increased (usually set to total memory in MB / 16384, e.g., 524288 for 8GB memory); 2. In high-concurrency short-connection scenarios, if nf_conntrack_count frequently approaches nf_conntrack_max, this value should be adjusted together with the connection tracking timeout parameters (nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_* series) to avoid prematurely filling the tracking table

kernel.pid_max.desc: - When the system frequently reaches the current pid_max limit causing inability to create new processes, this value should be appropriately increased, usually to 2-4 times the default value (32768). - In containerized environments requiring support for a large number of short-lived processes, it is recommended to increase pid_max to 262144 (2^18) to match the upper limit supported by modern Linux kernels

kernel.shmmni.desc: - When running databases requiring a large number of shared memory segments (e.g., Oracle) or scientific computing applications, if error logs related to 'SHMMNI' appear, this value should be increased to exceed the application's actual requirement by 20% redundancy. - In containerized or virtualized environments where a single physical node needs to host multiple shared memory-intensive instances, this value should be set to 1.5 times the number of instances multiplied by the requirement of a single instance

kernel.shmmax.desc: 1. When running applications requiring a large amount of shared memory (e.g., Oracle database, SAP HANA), if the application reports errors indicating insufficient shared memory, kernel.shmmax needs to be set to at least 80%-90% of the total sum of all shared memory segments, but not exceeding 90% of physical memory; 2. In containerized or virtualized environments, when multiple instances require shared memory communication and performance bottlenecks occur, kernel.shmmax should be adjusted based on the actual shared memory requirement sum of each instance, ensuring its value is greater than the sum of all instance requirements

kernel.shmall.desc: 1. When the system runs applications requiring a large amount of shared memory (e.g., Oracle database) and encounters 'SHMMAX too small' errors, this value needs to be increased to about 80% of physical memory; 2. When the system frequently uses shared memory but does not fully utilize physical memory, this value can be appropriately decreased to avoid resource waste, usually set to (Total Physical Memory - System Reserved Memory) / PAGE_SIZE

kernel.core_uses_pid.desc: 1. When needing to quickly locate crashing processes, it is recommended to enable this parameter (set to 1). The PID in the core filename allows quick association with specific process information; 2. When the system frequently generates core files and disk space is tight, it is recommended to disable this parameter (set to 0) to avoid management difficulties caused by long filenames

kernel.msgmni.desc: 1. When system logs frequently show 'msgmni limit reached' errors, it indicates the current number of queues is insufficient to support application demands, and this value needs to be increased; 2. For middleware applications that frequently use System V message queues (e.g., Oracle database), it is recommended to set this value to at least 4 times the number of processes

kernel.msgmax.desc: 1. When applications frequently send large messages exceeding the current kernel.msgmax limit, causing message queue operations to fail, this value should be appropriately increased, but ensure it does not exceed a reasonable proportion of available system memory; 2. If the system handles a large number of small messages and an excessively large msgmax setting leads to memory fragmentation, this value should be decreased to match the actual message size, usually not lower than 8KB

kernel.msgmnb.desc: Increase this value when message queues frequently reach the default upper limit (usually 16384 bytes) causing application errors. Decrease this value when the system has many idle message queues and needs to reduce kernel memory usage

kernel.hung_task_timeout_secs.desc: 1. When the system frequently reports hung_task warnings but tasks are actually executing normally, this value can be appropriately increased (e.g., from the default 120 seconds to 300 seconds) to avoid false positives; 2. For storage-intensive applications (e.g., database servers), if tasks frequently timeout due to slow storage device responses, this value should be increased to 2-3 times the average response time of the storage device, combined with storage latency metrics

kernel.nmi_watchdog.desc: 1. On production servers, it is recommended to disable this parameter (set to 0) because the NMI watchdog periodically triggers NMI interrupts, which may slightly impact system performance, especially under high load; 2. When debugging kernel deadlocks or hardware issues, it can be temporarily enabled (set to 1) to help capture hangs caused by long interrupt disables

kernel.sched_rt_runtime_us.desc: 1. When the system needs to run more real-time tasks, this value can be appropriately increased (but not exceeding 95% of sched_rt_period_us). The default value of 950000 microseconds can be increased to 990000 microseconds; 2. When non-real-time tasks experience severe starvation, this value should be decreased (recommended not lower than 800000 microseconds) to reserve more CPU time for ordinary tasks

kernel.timer_migration.desc: 1. On NUMA architecture servers running low-latency applications, if performance jitter occurs due to cross-node clock interrupts, this parameter should be disabled to keep clock interrupts handled by the local CPU; 2. When the system load is mainly concentrated on a single NUMA node and clock interrupt handling is unbalanced, this parameter can be enabled to allow clock interrupt migration between CPUs

kernel.threads-max.desc: 1. When the system frequently encounters 'fork: Cannot allocate memory' errors or applications crash due to inability to create new threads, this value needs to be increased. A reasonable upper limit can be determined by calculating system memory capacity and the average memory footprint per thread, usually set to Physical Memory (MB) / 8.; 2. In high-concurrency container environments or when running applications with many lightweight threads (e.g., Java microservices), if /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max has been increased but thread creation limits still exist, this value should be increased to at least 2 times the pid_max value

kernel.sysrq.desc: 1. In production environments, it is recommended to set it to 1 (only enable basic functions) or 0 (completely disable) to avoid accidentally triggering system operations via SysRq key combinations and reduce security risks; 2. When debugging crash or hang issues, temporarily set it to 1 or a larger value (e.g., 176/128) to enable more debugging functions, and immediately restore the default secure configuration afterwards

kernel.sched_autogroup_enabled.desc: 1. In server environments, it is recommended to disable this parameter (set to 0) because automatic task grouping is primarily optimized for desktop interactive programs, and server workloads typically do not require this scheduling feature; 2. When the server runs many short interactive tasks and experiences scheduling latency issues, enabling it (set to 1) can be tried to observe the effect, but note that it may affect the throughput of batch processing tasks

kernel.numa_balancing.desc: 1. When the system runs on NUMA architecture and applications have cross-node memory access, this parameter should be enabled (set to 1) to reduce remote memory access latency; 2. For memory-intensive and latency-sensitive applications, if a high proportion of cross-node memory access is observed, it is recommended to disable this parameter (set to 0) to avoid performance fluctuations caused by automatic balancing

kernel.randomize_va_space.desc: 1. When the system runs services with high security requirements, it is recommended to keep the default value of 2 (full randomization) to enhance resistance against memory attacks; 2. If applications experience compatibility issues due to address randomization and the runtime environment is trusted, it can be temporarily adjusted to 1 (only randomize data segments) or 0 (disable) for testing

kernel.dmesg_restrict.desc: 1. If the system needs to meet security compliance requirements (e.g., PCI-DSS, HIPAA), it is recommended to set it to 1 to restrict ordinary users from viewing kernel logs and prevent sensitive information leakage; 2. In environments requiring development debugging or troubleshooting, it is recommended to set it to 0 so that non-privileged users can also view complete system log information

vm.swappiness.desc: 1. For memory-intensive applications (e.g., databases, cache services), it is recommended to set vm.swappiness to 10-30 to reduce swap space usage and prioritize physical memory; 2. When the system frequently experiences OOM (Out of Memory), vm.swappiness can be appropriately increased to 60-80 to increase swap space usage and avoid processes being forcibly terminated

vm.vfs_cache_pressure.desc: 1. When the system frequently performs directory and inode cache reclamation leading to performance degradation, this value can be appropriately decreased (e.g., set to 50-100) to reduce the frequency of kernel reclaiming cached memory; 2. When system memory is sufficient but cache utilization is low, this value can be appropriately increased (e.g., set to 150-200) to prompt the kernel to more actively reclaim cached memory

vm.dirty_background_ratio.desc: 1. For write-intensive applications (e.g., database servers), it is recommended to increase the value from the default 10% to 15-20% to reduce the impact of frequent background flushes on I/O performance; 2. For systems with smaller memory (e.g., less than 8GB), it is recommended to keep the default value or decrease it to 5-10% to avoid excessive dirty page accumulation causing memory pressure

vm.dirty_ratio.desc: 1. When the system frequently experiences I/O bottlenecks due to dirty page flushing, this value can be appropriately decreased (e.g., from the default 20% to 10%) to reduce the amount of data flushed at once, but this will increase the flush frequency; 2. If the system has large memory and primarily handles sequential write loads, this value can be appropriately increased (e.g., to 30%-40%) to use memory to buffer more dirty data, reducing disk I/O次数

vm.stat_interval.desc: 1. When the system requires more frequent monitoring of memory usage (e.g., under high memory pressure or frequent swapping), this value can be appropriately decreased (e.g., from the default 10 seconds to 5 seconds), but note the increased system overhead; 2. In stable memory usage and low-load environments, this value can be increased (e.g., adjusted to 30 seconds) to reduce the update frequency of /proc/vmstat and lower kernel overhead

vm.dirty_expire_centisecs.desc: 1. For applications requiring fast data persistence (e.g., databases), it is recommended to lower the value to 100-300 (1-3 seconds) to reduce the risk of data loss; 2. For write-intensive workloads with latency-sensitive applications, it can be appropriately increased to 1000-3000 (10-30 seconds) to improve I/O throughput by merging more write operations

vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs.desc: 1. When the system frequently experiences I/O waits or high disk write latency, this value can be appropriately decreased (e.g., from the default 500 to 200-300) to speed up the dirty page writeback frequency and reduce performance fluctuations caused by burst writes; 2. For write-intensive workloads on battery-powered devices (e.g., server UPS environments), this value can be appropriately increased (e.g., set to 1000-1500) to reduce disk write frequency, lowering I/O overhead and energy consumption

vm.overcommit_ratio.desc: 1. When physical server memory usage is consistently below 50% and there is a need to run many applications with uncertain memory requests, this ratio can be appropriately increased (e.g., set to 80-90%) to improve memory utilization; 2. In memory-intensive application scenarios, if the OOM killer is frequently triggered and monitoring shows actual memory usage is close to the total physical memory, this ratio should be decreased (e.g., set to 50-70%) to avoid overcommitting memory

vm.overcommit_memory.desc: 1. When the system runs memory-intensive applications and frequently triggers the OOM killer, it is recommended to set the value to 0 (conservative policy) or 2 (strict policy) to avoid overallocation; 2. When the system primarily runs batch tasks with known memory requirements and needs to maximize memory utilization, it can be set to 1 (always allow overcommitment) to improve throughput

vm.min_free_kbytes.desc: 1. When the system frequently triggers direct memory reclaim leading to performance degradation, this value needs to be increased to reduce the frequency of direct reclaim. It is recommended to set it to 1-3% of physical memory; 2. When the system has a large number of unmovable pages causing severe memory fragmentation, this value should be appropriately increased to reserve more contiguous memory space

vm.page-cluster.desc: 1. When the system frequently performs large contiguous memory swapping, this value can be appropriately increased (default 3, recommended range 3-10) to reduce the I/O overhead of swap operations; 2. In SSD swap partition environments, due to better random access performance, this value can be decreased (recommended 1-3) to reduce single swap latency

vm.max_map_count.desc: Increase this value when running memory-intensive applications (like Elasticsearch or databases) and encountering the error 'max virtual memory areas vm.max_map_count [65530] is too low'. Set this value to 262144 or higher when running Java applications that require a large number of memory mappings (like Hadoop or Spark)

vm.zone_reclaim_mode.desc: 1. When the system runs on NUMA architecture and experiences cross-node memory access latency issues, it is recommended to set vm.zone_reclaim_mode to 1, prioritizing memory reclamation on the local node to reduce remote access latency; 2. When the system is under high memory pressure and local node reclamation is ineffective, it is recommended to set vm.zone_reclaim_mode to 0, allowing memory reclamation from other nodes to improve overall reclamation efficiency

vm.watermark_scale_factor.desc: 1. When the system frequently triggers direct memory reclaim and the kswapd process activity is insufficient, this value can be appropriately decreased (e.g., from the default 10 to 5-8) to make kswapd intervene in memory reclamation earlier; 2. Under high memory pressure scenarios where kswapd runs continuously, if increased system response latency is observed, try increasing this value (e.g., adjust to 15-20) to delay kswapd's sleep timing and improve reclamation efficiency

vm.numa_stat.desc: 1. When system memory resources are tight and NUMA statistics are not critical for the current business scenario, this parameter can be set to 0 to reduce statistical accuracy and decrease memory overhead; 2. In high-performance computing scenarios requiring precise monitoring of NUMA memory behavior, this parameter should remain enabled (default value 1) to obtain complete statistical information

vm.drop_caches.desc: 1. When system memory pressure is high and cache usage is excessive, it can be temporarily set to 3 to release pagecache, dentries, and inodes caches, but frequent operation is not advisable as it may affect performance; 2. Before running memory-intensive applications, it can be set to 1 to release only pagecache, avoiding cache interference with application performance test results

fs.inotify.max_user_watches.desc: 1. When monitoring a large number of files or directories (e.g., log directories, code repositories), if errors like 'Too many open files' or 'User limit of inotify watches reached' occur, this value needs to be increased; 2. For high-concurrency file monitoring scenarios (e.g., real-time log analysis, file synchronization services), it is recommended to adjust this value to 4-8 times the default value (usually 8192). The specific value should be determined based on the actual number of monitored files

fs.nr_open.desc: 1. When applications (e.g., databases, Web servers) frequently report 'too many open files' errors and ulimit -n has already been increased, this value needs to be increased to be greater than or equal to the maximum number of file descriptors actually needed by the process; 2. In systems with tight memory resources, if this value is set too high (e.g., close to the memlock limit), it should be appropriately decreased to prevent memory exhaustion

fs.file-max.desc: 1. When the system frequently encounters 'Too many open files' errors or monitoring shows file handle usage consistently approaching the current limit, this value needs to be increased; 2. For high-concurrency services (e.g., Web servers, databases), it is recommended to set this value to 10%-20% of the physical memory size in KB (e.g., for 64GB memory, set to 6,400,000-12,800,000)

fs.aio-max-nr.desc: - When system logs frequently show 'aio-max-nr reached' warnings or applications report errors due to rejected asynchronous I/O requests, this value needs to be increased. - For high-concurrency database servers (e.g., MySQL/PostgreSQL) or large-scale file processing applications, it is recommended to set this value to (number of concurrent threads × number of outstanding AIO requests each thread may hold) × 2

fs.inotify.max_user_instances.desc: 1. When system logs frequently show 'inotify instance limit reached' or similar errors, it indicates that the number of monitoring processes (e.g., file synchronization tools, development hot-reload tools) run by the current user exceeds the limit, and this value needs to be increased; 2. In environments running many containers or microservices, where each container instance may require an independent inotify instance to monitor file changes, this parameter should be reasonably increased based on the actual number of containers

fs.suid_dumpable.desc: 1. When the system needs to debug setuid program crash issues, it is recommended to set the value to 1 (debug mode), allowing core dump files to be generated for fault analysis; 2. In production environments focused on security, it is recommended to keep the default value of 0 to avoid potential security risks and prevent sensitive information leakage through core dumps

blockdev.desc: Increasing the read-ahead value (e.g., setting it to 8192) can improve sequential read performance, suitable for scenarios involving frequent large file sequential reads. Decreasing the read-ahead value (e.g., setting it to 128) can reduce I/O overhead, suitable for scenarios dominated by random access

block.fifo_batch.desc: 1. When the system requires higher throughput and can tolerate higher latency (e.g., batch data processing scenarios), this value can be appropriately increased (e.g., 32-64); 2. When the system is latency-sensitive (e.g., real-time databases) and current throughput is sufficient, this value can be decreased (e.g., 8-12) to reduce the processing latency of a single batch

block.front_merges.desc: 1. When the I/O load primarily comes from sequential writes and the storage device performs well, it is recommended to keep the default value of 1 to allow forward merging, which can reduce the number of requests and improve throughput; 2. When the system handles a large amount of random I/O or experiences performance degradation with certain storage devices, try setting this parameter to 0 to disable forward merging and reduce unnecessary merge operation overhead

block.read_expire.desc: 1. When the system primarily handles high-priority read operations (e.g., database queries) and has read latency-sensitive applications, this value can be appropriately decreased (e.g., from the default 125ms to 50-100ms) to ensure read requests are responded to faster; 2. If the system frequently experiences read request timeout discards (detectable by monitoring the deadline scheduler's statistics) and the storage device's actual response capability is better than the current setting, this value should be appropriately increased (e.g., to 150-200ms) to avoid unnecessary request retries

block.writes_starved.desc: 1. When the system primarily handles random read-intensive loads (e.g., database services) and requires low-latency responses, this value can be appropriately increased (default range 2-5) to prioritize read requests and reduce read latency; 2. When the system has a large number of sequential write operations (e.g., log writing, data backup) and write performance becomes a bottleneck, this value should be decreased (minimum can be set to 1) to prevent read requests from excessively preempting I/O bandwidth and affecting write throughput

block.max_sectors_kb.desc: 1. When using high-performance storage devices (e.g., NVMe SSD) and there are many large-block I/O operations, this value can be appropriately increased (e.g., 1024-4096 KB) to improve throughput; 2. When I/O errors occur or the device driver is unstable, this value should be decreased to the default 512 KB or lower to enhance stability

block.queue_depth.desc: 1. When using high-performance storage devices (e.g., NVMe SSD) and the system is under high load, if storage device utilization is insufficient or IOPS do not meet expectations, this value can be appropriately increased (usually recommended to gradually increase from the default 32 to the range of 64-256), but ensure it does not exceed the device's hardware queue depth limit; 2. For virtual machine environments or low-performance spinning disks (e.g., HDD), if latency increases significantly or request timeouts occur, the value should be decreased to the range of 16-32 to reduce I/O backlog

block.nr_requests.desc: 1. When the system has high-performance storage devices (e.g., NVMe SSD) and IOPS throughput is insufficient, this value can be appropriately increased (default 128), recommended range 256-1024, to fully utilize the device's parallel processing capability; 2. When the system experiences high latency or request backlog, if the storage device is a mechanical hard drive, this value should be decreased (recommended 64-128) to avoid increased seek time due to overly deep single device queues

block.read_ahead_kb.desc: 1. When the system primarily runs applications that sequentially read large files (e.g., databases, video streaming services) and memory is sufficient, this value can be appropriately increased (e.g., from the default 128KB to 512KB-1MB) to reduce I/O wait time; 2. When the system is under memory pressure or primarily handles random access loads, this value should be decreased (e.g., adjusted to 64KB or lower) to avoid pre-reading too much useless data occupying precious memory resources

block.rq_affinity.desc: 1. When the system experiences unbalanced CPU utilization under high I/O load, it is recommended to adjust this parameter to improve the efficiency of local CPU processing I/O requests; 2. When using multi-queue storage devices, if I/O performance does not meet expectations, it is recommended to adjust this parameter to fully utilize the parallel processing capability of multi-core CPUs

block.add_random.desc: 1. When the system requires extremely high random number quality and performance overhead is acceptable, it is recommended to enable this parameter to enhance the randomness source of the entropy pool; 2. In high-performance computing or low-latency scenarios, if the system already has sufficient entropy sources, it is recommended to disable this parameter to avoid additional overhead from I/O events

block.rotational.desc: 1. When the storage device is an SSD, this parameter must be set to 0 to prevent the system from incorrectly applying I/O scheduling policies intended for mechanical hard drives; 2. When the storage device is a mechanical hard drive, this parameter should remain at the default value of 1 to ensure the system correctly applies relevant optimizations suitable for rotating media

block.scheduler.desc: 1. For MySQL database scenarios, it is recommended to set block.scheduler to 'deadline'. This scheduling algorithm can better handle the random I/O load of databases and reduce I/O latency; 2. If the system uses SSD storage devices, consider setting the scheduler to 'noop' because SSDs have no seek time of mechanical disks, and simple FIFO queue scheduling can achieve optimal performance

block.write_cache.desc: 1. When the system requires higher write performance and can tolerate a small risk of data loss, it is recommended to set it to write back mode; 2. When data security requirements are extremely high and performance is not the primary consideration, it is recommended to set it to write through mode

block.nomerges.desc: 1. Set to 0 only when debugging I/O request merging related issues. The production environment should keep the default value of 1 to benefit from the performance advantages of merging; 2. When using tools like blktrace for low-level block device analysis, merging can be temporarily disabled (set to 0) to obtain more accurate request tracking data

net.core.netdev_budget.desc: 1. When network interfaces frequently experience packet drops (ifconfig shows increasing RX dropped) and CPU soft interrupt (softirq) usage is high, it is recommended to appropriately increase this value (default 300 can be tried to adjust to 600-800) to increase the number of packets processed per soft interrupt and reduce interrupt frequency; 2. In low-throughput but latency-sensitive scenarios (e.g., high-frequency trading systems), if network latency fluctuates, try decreasing this value (e.g., adjust to 150-200) to reduce the processing time per soft interrupt and lower processing latency

net.core.optmem_max.desc: - When applications (such as high-performance network services) need to handle a large number of concurrent connections or high-capacity data, and performance bottlenecks occur due to insufficient socket buffers, this value can be appropriately increased. - On servers with ample memory resources, if the default value (usually 20480) cannot meet the needs of specific applications (such as video streaming, big data transmission), gradually increase it in powers of 2 to a reasonable range (e.g., 65536 or 131072)

net.core.wmem_max.desc: 1. When the server handles a large number of high-throughput network connections (e.g., video streaming, large file transfer scenarios) and experiences performance bottlenecks due to insufficient write buffers, it is recommended to change the value from the default 229376 to 16777216; 2. In high-concurrency TCP long-connection scenarios (e.g., WebSocket services, message queues), if connection abnormalities or data loss are observed due to write buffer overflow, it is recommended to use the value 16777216

net.core.wmem_default.desc: 1. When the application primarily handles a large number of small data packet transmissions, if network throughput is lower than expected and system monitoring shows the send buffer frequently fills up, this value can be appropriately increased to the range of 32768-65535 bytes to reduce latency caused by frequent buffer filling; 2. In high-bandwidth, high-latency network environments (e.g., cross-data center transmission), if the TCP window scaling function is enabled but the actual window is still limited by the default value, this value should be increased to at least 163840 bytes (160KB) to match the BDP (Bandwidth-Delay Product) requirement

net.core.rmem_default.desc: 1. When the application needs to handle a large amount of network data flow (e.g., video streaming, big data transmission) and frequent TCP window scaling or retransmission is observed, it is recommended to increase the value from the default 212992 bytes to the range of 1-4 MB (1048576-4194304 bytes), and adjust net.core.rmem_max simultaneously; 2. In high-throughput, low-latency network environments (e.g., 10Gbps and above), if netstat -s shows continuous growth in 'pruned' or 'collapsed' packet statistics, it is recommended to set the value to 1/4 to 1/2 of the BDP (Bandwidth-Delay Product). Calculation formula: (Bandwidth(bps) × Round-trip Time(s)) / 8 × 0.25

net.core.rmem_max.desc: 1. When the application needs to handle high-throughput network data flows (e.g., video streaming, big data transmission), this value should be adjusted to 16777216 to improve receiving performance; 2. When there are a large number of TCP long connections and frequent warnings about insufficient receive buffers (e.g., kernel logs report 'TCP: too much of memory'), this value should be increased

net.core.netdev_max_backlog.desc: 1. When the server frequently experiences network packet loss or high load, and monitoring shows the netdev_backlog value consistently approaches or reaches the current netdev_max_backlog setting, this parameter value should be appropriately increased (e.g., from the default 1000 to 2000-3000); 2. For 10Gbps and higher-speed network interfaces, if the default value causes increased data packet processing latency, this parameter value needs to be increased proportionally based on the actual network throughput and CPU processing capability

net.ipv4.tcp_thin_linear_timeouts.desc: 1. When the server handles a large number of short-lived TCP connections and frequently experiences timeout retransmissions, it is recommended to enable this parameter (tcp_thin_linear_timeouts=1) to more accurately detect thin streams and reduce unnecessary retransmission wait times; 2. If the server primarily handles large file transfers or video streaming and other sustained high-throughput connections, it is recommended to keep the default value (tcp_thin_linear_timeouts=0) to avoid misjudging normal data flows

net.unix.max_dgram_qlen.desc: 1. When the system frequently handles a large number of UDP datagrams and experiences packet loss, consider increasing this value to improve queue capacity; 2. In high-throughput UDP application scenarios, if the application processing speed cannot keep up with the data receiving speed, leading to queue overflow, this parameter should be appropriately increased

net.core.somaxconn.desc: 1. When the server needs to handle a large number of concurrent connection requests (e.g., high-load Web servers) and experiences connection drops or queuing delays, this value should be increased from the default 128 to 1024 or higher; 2. When running services that frequently establish short connections (e.g., reverse proxies, load balancers), it is recommended to adjust this value to at least equal to or greater than 1/4 of the product of the service's worker_processes and worker_connections

net.core.busy_poll.desc: 1. In high-throughput network environments (e.g., 10Gbps and above), if CPU utilization is insufficient and there are latency-sensitive applications, this value can be appropriately increased (e.g., 50-100 microseconds) to reduce interrupt frequency, but CPU load must be monitored to avoid excessive occupation; 2. In low-latency network environments (e.g., high-frequency trading systems), if network latency indicators do not meet standards and CPU resources are sufficient, try setting it to 0 to disable this function, forcing the use of interrupt mode to reduce latency

net.core.busy_read.desc: 1. When network devices handle high-throughput small packets and experience frequent read timeouts or performance degradation, try increasing this value to the range of 100-200 microseconds. The optimal value needs to be determined by testing combined with specific hardware performance; 2. In low-latency network environments, if abnormal CPU usage increase is observed and related to network interrupt processing, test decreasing this value to 20-30 microseconds to reduce waiting time

net.core.dev_weight.desc: 1. When network interrupt processing becomes a performance bottleneck (monitoring shows high CPU soft interrupt time percentage), this value can be appropriately increased to increase the number of data packets processed per interrupt, but care must be taken to avoid overloading a single CPU; 2. For high-throughput network cards (e.g., 10G/25G and above) or scenarios with many small packets, it is recommended to increase this value from the default 64 to the range of 128-256. The optimal value needs to be determined by testing based on specific hardware and load

net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_intvl.desc: 1. When the server needs to detect the health status of long-idle connections, if the default value of 75 seconds causes high fault detection delay, it can be appropriately decreased to the range of 30-60 seconds to speed up fault discovery, but the impact of increased network load must be weighed; 2. In high-latency network environments, if false connection interruptions frequently occur, consider increasing this value to the range of 90-120 seconds to reduce unnecessary probe traffic, while ensuring the overall detection window is reasonable by adjusting tcp_keepalive_probes accordingly

net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_probes.desc: 1. When the server needs to quickly detect and release failed connections (e.g., load balancer backend health check scenarios), this value (default 9) can be appropriately reduced. It is recommended to adjust to 3-5 times to speed up the recycling of failed connections; 2. In high-latency or unreliable network environments (e.g., cross-border VPN), to prevent misjudging active connections as failed, this value should be increased to 12-15 times, while adjusting the tcp_keepalive_time and tcp_keepalive_intvl parameters accordingly

net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time.desc: 1. When the server needs to detect the validity of long-idle connections (e.g., load balancer or reverse proxy scenarios), if the default value (7200 seconds) is too long and may cause invalid connections to occupy resources, it can be appropriately reduced to the range of 300-600 seconds; 2. In high-concurrency short-connection business scenarios, if a large number of TIME_WAIT state connections cause port exhaustion, this parameter value can be increased to above 10800 seconds by reducing the tcp_keepalive_probes and tcp_keepalive_intvl parameters to decrease the keepalive probe frequency

net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse.desc: 1. When the server faces a large number of short connection requests and too many TIME-WAIT state connections cause port exhaustion, it is recommended to enable this parameter (set to 1) to reuse TIME-WAIT sockets; 2. In NAT network environments or scenarios requiring strict TCP connection reliability, it is recommended to keep this parameter at the default value of 0 to avoid potential connection confusion risks

net.ipv4.tcp_window_scaling.desc: 1. In high-bandwidth or high-latency network environments (e.g., long-distance transmission or high-speed networks), ensure this parameter value is 1 to enable the window scaling function and improve large-window TCP connection performance; 2. When network devices do not support RFC 1323 or have compatibility issues, this parameter should be set to 0 to disable the window scaling function

net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout.desc: 1. When the server needs to handle a large number of short connection requests, if a large number of connections are observed in the FIN_WAIT_2 state causing port exhaustion, it is recommended to reduce this value from the default 60 seconds to 30 seconds or lower to speed up connection resource release; 2. For high-latency network environments or application scenarios that require maintaining long-term connections, if abnormal connection termination issues are found, it is recommended to appropriately increase this value to above 120 seconds to ensure normal connection closure

net.ipv4.udp_mem.desc: 1. When the server frequently handles a large amount of UDP traffic (e.g., DNS servers, video streaming servers) and experiences packet loss or performance degradation, the high value can be appropriately increased (e.g., 2-3 times the default value) to ensure sufficient memory buffers for queue data packets; 2. If the system has ample free memory but UDP applications still frequently trigger pressure mode (observable by monitoring /proc/net/sockstat), the low and assure values should be increased proportionally (e.g., low set to 1% of total memory, assure set to 2%) to avoid unnecessary memory reclamation抖动

net.ipv4.tcp_mem.desc: 1. When the system experiences memory shortage or frequently triggers the OOM killer under high-concurrency TCP connection scenarios, the three values (min pressure value/pressure threshold/max value) should be appropriately increased. It is recommended to calculate based on 1%-3% of the total physical memory, ensuring the max value does not exceed 50% of the system's available memory; 2. If the system experiences TCP performance degradation or connection refusal (especially in high-throughput scenarios), check if the current value is too small. It is recommended to set the min value to 1.5 times the memory footprint of current active connections, and the max value to 30%-40% of the system's free memory

net.ipv4.tcp_rmem.desc: 1. In high-throughput network environments (e.g., video streaming servers, big data transfer nodes), when the default maximum value of 6291456 (6MB) causes the TCP receive window to become a bottleneck, it is recommended to adjust the third value to 16777216 (16MB) to improve throughput; 2. For servers with limited memory resources (e.g., cloud hosts or container environments), if the default initial buffer value of 87380 (85KB) causes memory pressure, the middle value can be reduced to 65536 (64KB) to balance performance and resource consumption

net.ipv4.tcp_wmem.desc: 1. In high-throughput network environments (e.g., video streaming servers, file transfer servers), it is recommended to adjust the parameter to 4096 65536 16777216 to enhance TCP write buffer performance in high-traffic scenarios; 2. For servers with limited memory resources (e.g., cloud hosts or container environments), if memory pressure occurs, the maximum value should be appropriately reduced (e.g., adjusted to 4096 32768 8388608) to prevent TCP write buffers from occupying too much memory

net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen.desc: 1. When the server primarily handles a large number of short connection requests (e.g., HTTP API services) and needs to reduce TCP handshake latency, it is recommended to enable this parameter (value 3 supports both client and server sides); 2. When the server is in a strict security environment or handles sensitive data, it is recommended to disable this parameter (value 0) to avoid potential security risks

net.ipv4.tcp_synack_retries.desc: 1. When the server is in a high-concurrency connection scenario and has many SYN_RECV state connections, if network latency is high, this value (default 5) can be appropriately increased to 7-10 times to ensure the three-way handshake completes in congested environments; 2. If the server is under SYN Flood attack or high load, this value can be decreased to 2-3 times to quickly release half-open connection resources and reduce SYN queue occupation time

net.ipv4.tcp_syn_retries.desc: 1. In high-latency or unstable network environments (e.g., cross-border networks or mobile networks), it is recommended to appropriately increase the default value of 6 to 8-10 to handle possible SYN packet loss, but note this will extend the wait time when connection establishment fails; 2. For internal networks or low-latency, high-reliability network environments, it is recommended to decrease it to 3-4 to reduce connection establishment timeout wait time and improve application response speed

net.ipv4.tcp_moderate_rcvbuf.desc: 1. When the application needs to handle a large amount of burst traffic, it is recommended to enable this parameter (set to 1). The system will automatically adjust the receive buffer size to adapt to traffic changes; 2. In memory-constrained environments, it is recommended to disable this parameter (set to 0) to prevent the system from automatically expanding the receive buffer and increasing memory pressure

net.ipv4.tcp_timestamps.desc: 1. In network environments with NAT devices or load balancers, it is recommended to disable this parameter (set to 0) to avoid potential connection issues caused by timestamp conflicts; 2. In high-speed, low-latency internal network environments, it is recommended to enable this parameter (set to 1) to obtain more accurate RTT calculations and better TCP performance

net.ipv4.tcp_dsack.desc: 1. In latency-sensitive application environments (e.g., high-frequency trading systems), it is recommended to set to 0 (disabled) to reduce unnecessary ACK confirmation packet network overhead; 2. In常规Web services or file transfer scenarios, keep the default value of 1 (enabled) to help handle data retransmission efficiency in case of network packet loss

net.ipv4.tcp_fack.desc: 1. In network environments with high latency or high packet loss rates, it is recommended to enable this parameter to improve TCP retransmission performance by reducing unnecessary retransmissions through selective acknowledgment; 2. When the server acts as the receiving end for high-performance network applications (e.g., video streaming, large file transfers), it is recommended to keep it enabled to optimize the TCP congestion control mechanism

net.ipv4.tcp_sack.desc: 1. In wide area network (WAN) communication environments, it should remain enabled (1), which can significantly improve TCP transmission performance in high-latency or packet loss networks, even if it slightly increases CPU load; 2. In low-latency, high-bandwidth local area network (LAN) environments, consider disabling (0), especially when the system CPU resources are highly saturated and network quality is excellent

net.ipv4.tcp_low_latency.desc: Should be enabled (set to 1) in high-throughput and latency-sensitive cluster environments (such as Beowulf clusters). Should remain disabled (set to 0) in ordinary network environments to avoid unnecessary overhead

net.ipv4.tcp_adv_win_scale.desc: 1. When the application needs to handle a large amount of small packet network traffic and observes insufficient TCP receive window utilization, consider increasing this value (e.g., set to 2 or 3) to reduce the buffer overhead ratio and improve small packet transmission efficiency; 2. In server environments with tight memory resources, if high TCP memory consumption is found causing frequent system OOM, this value can be appropriately decreased (e.g., set to 1 or 0) to increase the buffer overhead ratio and reduce memory usage

net.ipv4.route.max_size.desc: 1. When the server frequently handles a large number of network connections or acts as a router forwarding a large number of data packets, and observes performance degradation due to frequent routing cache refreshes, this value can be appropriately increased (the default value of 4096 can be gradually doubled for testing); 2. In high memory pressure environments, if the routing table occupies too much memory affecting other services, and the actual active routing entries are far below the current setting, this value can be appropriately decreased to free up memory

net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets.desc: 1. When the server has a large number of TIME_WAIT state TCP connections causing port exhaustion or performance degradation, it is recommended to adjust net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets from the default value of 2048 to 360000.; 2. In high-concurrency short-connection scenarios, if monitoring finds that the number of TIME_WAIT connections frequently reaches the upper limit, this value can be appropriately increased to 360000 to improve connection processing capability

net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog.desc: 1. When the server frequently handles a large number of new connection requests and experiences SYN packet drops, consider increasing this value to 8192 or higher; 2. In high-concurrency short-connection scenarios, if monitoring finds that the number of SYN_RECV state connections often approaches the default value of 2048, this parameter should be adjusted to avoid connection establishment delays

net.ipv4.tcp_max_orphans.desc: 1. When the server frequently encounters 'Out of socket memory' errors or logs show many orphaned sockets warnings, this value needs to be increased. It is recommended to adjust based on the current system memory capacity, usually set to the number of sockets corresponding to 1/4 of the memory capacity (each orphan occupies about 64KB of memory); 2. For high-concurrency short-connection services (e.g., HTTP servers, load balancers), if observing that the tcp_max_orphans limit becomes a performance bottleneck (by monitoring /proc/net/sockstat, the number of orphans is close to the upper limit), this value should be appropriately increased to 1.2-1.5 times the number of concurrent connections

net.ipv4.tcp_ecn.desc: 1. When there are outdated network devices in the network that do not support ECN, it is recommended to keep the default value of 0 (disabled) to avoid potential packet drop issues; 2. In environments where network devices fully support ECN and there is a need to reduce TCP retransmission rates, it is recommended to set it to 1 (enabled) to obtain better congestion control performance

net.ipv4.ip_forward.desc: - When the server needs to act as a router or VPN gateway, it should be set to 1 to enable IPv4 forwarding function. - When the server is only used as an end host, it should keep the default value of 0 to disable forwarding function and reduce potential security risks

net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter.desc: 1. When the server acts as a router or needs to handle multi-path network traffic, it is recommended to set rp_filter to 2 (loose mode) to avoid legitimate traffic being dropped due to strict reverse path verification; 2. On single-NIC servers in trusted network environments, it can be set to 0 (turn off verification) to reduce kernel processing overhead, but ensure there is no IP spoofing risk in the network environment

net.ipv4.tcp_no_metrics_save.desc: 1. In high-concurrency short-connection scenarios, it is recommended to set to 1 to disable TCP connection parameter saving, avoiding memory waste and performance degradation caused by a large number of invalid parameter caches; 2. In scenarios requiring long-connection stability, it is recommended to keep the default value of 0, allowing reuse of effective parameters from previous connections to optimize new connection establishment performance

net.ipv4.ip_default_ttl.desc: 1. When there are multiple layers of NAT or complex routing environments in the network, if data packets are discarded prematurely, consider increasing the TTL value to 128 to ensure data packets can reach more distant network nodes; 2. For scenarios that need to limit the propagation range of data packets (e.g., internal test networks), the TTL value can be reduced to 32 or below to prevent excessive propagation of data packets in the network

net.ipv4.ip_no_pmtu_disc.desc: 1. When there are Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) issues in the network causing connection timeouts or performance degradation, it is recommended to set this parameter to 1 to disable PMTUD, avoiding connection problems caused by ICMP black holes or firewall packet drops; 2. In high-speed network environments (e.g., 10Gbps and above) where network devices reliably support PMTUD, it is recommended to keep the default value of 0 to enable PMTUD, ensuring TCP can dynamically discover the optimal MTU value to improve throughput

net.ipv4.tcp_retries2.desc: 1. For servers in high-latency or unstable network environments, consider reducing the value to 5-8 to reduce the problem of connections hanging for long periods due to temporary network failures; 2. For financial transaction servers that need to quickly detect connection failures, it is recommended to set it to 3-5 to ensure faster release of failed connection resources

net.ipv4.tcp_orphan_retries.desc: 1. When the server faces a large number of half-open connections (orphaned sockets) causing high resource occupation, this value can be appropriately decreased (e.g., 3-5) to accelerate resource release, but note that too low may cause normal long-latency network connections to be prematurely discarded; 2. If the server primarily handles local or low-latency network communication and experiences excessive retries wasting resources, it can be reduced to 2-3 times to reduce unnecessary waiting time

net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies.desc: 1. When the server is frequently under SYN flood attacks, this parameter should be enabled (set to 1) to protect system resources from being exhausted; 2. In normal network environments without attacks, it is recommended to keep the default value (usually 1), because enabling syncookies may slightly decrease TCP connection performance

net.ipv4.tcp_reordering.desc: 1. When the network path has high packet loss rates or frequent reordering, and a significant increase in TCP retransmission rate and throughput decrease are observed, consider appropriately increasing this value (default 3 can be tried to adjust to 9-12) to tolerate more out-of-order packets rather than incorrectly triggering fast retransmission; 2. In low-latency network environments (e.g., inside data centers) using TSO/GRO and other offload technologies, if kernel logs frequently show 'TCP: too many of order packets' warnings, this value can be moderately decreased (e.g., adjusted to 6-8) to reduce out-of-order queue memory usage

net.ipv4.tcp_retrans_collapse.desc: 1. In Linux server environments, if it is confirmed that there are no old printer devices requiring compatibility, it is recommended to disable this parameter to optimize TCP retransmission performance; 2. When network throughput abnormally decreases and other factors are ruled out, try disabling this parameter to observe if it is caused by printer compatibility features

net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control.desc: 1. In high-bandwidth, high-latency network environments (e.g., cross-data center communication), it is recommended to switch the default 'cubic' algorithm to 'bbr', which can better utilize bandwidth and reduce queuing delay; 2. In wireless or mobile network environments, if frequent packet loss occurs, it is recommended to use 'vegas' or 'westwood' algorithms, as these algorithms more accurately distinguish packet loss and can avoid misjudging congestion

net.ipv4.conf.default.promote_secondarie.desc: 1. When the server needs to maintain high availability and relies on multiple IP addresses, it is recommended to set it to 1 to ensure that when the primary IP is removed, the secondary IP can be automatically promoted to primary IP to avoid service interruption; 2. In environments with strict security requirements, it is recommended to set it to 0 to ensure that when the primary IP is removed, all associated IPs are cleared to prevent potential security risks

net.ipv4.conf.all.promote_secondaries.desc: 1. When the server needs to maintain high availability and relies on multiple IP addresses, it is recommended to set it to 1 to ensure that when the primary IP is removed, the secondary IP can be automatically promoted to primary IP to avoid service interruption; 2. When the server's IP address management needs to strictly follow change control processes, it is recommended to keep the default value of 0 to ensure any IP address changes require explicit operations, preventing accidental configuration changes

net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects.desc: 1. For Linux servers used as gateways or routers, it is recommended to set it to 0 to disable ICMP redirect messages and prevent potential network topology spoofing attacks; 2. For ordinary host servers, if the network environment is trusted and the ICMP redirect function is needed to optimize routing, the default value of 1 can be kept; otherwise, it is recommended to set it to 0 to enhance security

net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects.desc: 1. When used as a router, it is recommended to set it to 0 to disable ICMP redirect messages and prevent potential network topology confusion and security risks; 2. When used as an end host, the default value of 1 can be kept to accept redirect messages, but if the network environment has high security requirements, it is recommended to also set it to 0

net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects.desc: - In production environments with high security requirements, it is recommended to set to 0 to disable and avoid potential security risks. - If the network environment requires receiving specific ICMP redirects and the gateway is trusted, it can be set to 1 but must be combined with other security measures

net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects.desc: 1. In production environments with high security requirements, it is recommended to set to 0 to prevent potential network redirect attacks; 2. If the server needs to receive ICMP redirect messages from trusted gateways to optimize routing, it can be set to 1

net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts.desc: 1. If the server is in a network environment that may suffer ICMP broadcast storm attacks (such as public networks or DMZ zones), it is recommended to set to 1 to avoid resource exhaustion; 2. If the server is located in a protected internal network and needs to receive ICMP broadcasts (such as network device discovery scenarios), it is recommended to set to 0 to maintain normal functionality

net.nf_conntrack_max.desc: 1. When the server handles a large number of network connections (e.g., high-concurrency proxies, NAT gateways, or firewalls) and frequently encounters 'nf_conntrack: table full' logs, this value needs to be increased to avoid connection tracking table overflow; 2. When the system memory is insufficient and the connection tracking table utilization is consistently below 50%, this value can be appropriately decreased to free up memory resources

net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_e.desc: 1. When the server handles a large number of persistent TCP connections (e.g., long-connection services, proxy servers, etc.) and observes frequent nf_conntrack table full conditions leading to packet loss, this value can be appropriately increased (default 43200 seconds/12 hours), but ensure it does not exceed the client's actual connection hold time to avoid invalid connections occupying resources; 2. For Web server environments primarily handling short connections, if system memory pressure is high and connection tracking table usage is excessive, this value can be appropriately decreased (but should not be less than 1800 seconds) to accelerate connection entry recycling

net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_c.desc: 1. When the server handles a large number of short connections and frequently encounters close_wait states, if this value is too large (default 240 seconds), it will cause connection resources to be occupied for a long time and can be appropriately decreased to the range of 60-120 seconds; 2. For server environments primarily handling long connections, if abnormal connection disconnections cause resource leaks, consider increasing this value to the range of 300-600 seconds

net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_f.desc: 1. When the server handles a large number of short connections and frequently encounters FIN_WAIT state connection backlog, if system logs show frequent nf_conntrack table full conditions leading to packet loss, this value can be appropriately reduced to the range of 30-60 seconds to accelerate connection recycling; 2. If the server primarily handles long connections and the number of concurrent connections is far below 80% of nf_conntrack_max, and FIN_WAIT state connections timeout prematurely causing abnormal disconnections, this value can be increased to the range of 120-300 seconds to ensure normal connection termination processes complete

net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_t.desc: 1. When the server handles a large number of short connections and encounters many TIME_WAIT state connections causing the nf_conntrack table to fill up, this value (default 120 seconds) can be appropriately decreased. It is recommended to adjust to 30-60 seconds to release connection tracking entries faster; 2. If the server acts as a reverse proxy or load balancer and encounters port exhaustion issues, and after confirming there is no risk of retransmission packets, consider decreasing this value to 15-30 seconds, but ensure it is greater than TCP's 2MSL time

net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding.desc: 1. When the server needs to act as a router or gateway to forward IPv4 traffic, this parameter should be set to 1; otherwise, keep the default value of 0 to turn off the forwarding function and improve security; 2. In container or virtualization environments, if the host machine needs to provide network forwarding functionality for virtual machines/containers, this parameter needs to be enabled

net.core.rps_sock_flow_entries.desc: 1. When the server handles a large number of network connections and the RPS/RFS function is enabled, if CPU cache hit rates decrease or network latency increases, consider increasing this value (usually recommended to set to 32768 or 65536); 2. In high-throughput network environments (e.g., 10Gbps and above), if network performance does not meet expectations and /proc/net/softnet_stat shows increasing drop counts, this value should be adjusted to at least equal to or greater than the expected number of concurrent connections

net.ipv4.tcp_min_tso_segs.desc: 1. When the server primarily handles a large number of small data packets (e.g., less than 1460 bytes) and TSO utilization is low, this value (default 2) can be appropriately decreased to reduce latency, but ensure it is not lower than 1 to avoid performance degradation; 2. For high-speed networks (10Gbps+) and large data transfer scenarios, if insufficient TSO segmentation is observed causing high CPU utilization, this value can be appropriately increased (recommended not to exceed 8) to improve throughput

net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects.desc: 1. For general-purpose host servers, the recommended value is 0; if packet forwarding is not enabled, this feature should remain disabled. 2. For servers acting as routers, it is recommended to set this to 1 to enable ICMP redirect messages, helping hosts optimize routing decisions

net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects.desc: 1. This kernel parameter controls whether ICMP redirect messages are sent for the default outgoing network interface. Compared to net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects, this setting applies specifically to newly created interfaces. The recommended value is 0 to prevent external entities from modifying the system's routing table, which could be exploited for network attacks or spoofing. 2. For servers functioning as routers, it is recommended to set this to 1 to enable ICMP redirect messages, helping hosts optimize routing decisions

net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_respons.desc: 1. This kernel parameter controls whether bogus ICMP error responses are ignored. The recommended value is 1 to improve system security and prevent attackers from exploiting forged error messages for network-based attacks. 2. It should only be temporarily set to 0 in rare debugging scenarios, and must be reverted afterward

net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter.desc: 1. This kernel parameter controls whether IP reverse path filtering is enabled. The recommended value is 1 to enhance network security. Enabling reverse path filtering helps mitigate common network attacks, especially those involving IP address spoofing. 2. It should only be temporarily set to 0 in rare debugging scenarios, and must be reverted afterward

net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects.desc: 1. This kernel parameter controls whether IPv6 redirect messages are accepted. The recommended value is 0 to enhance system security. Disabling IPv6 redirects prevents attackers from performing man-in-the-middle attacks or traffic hijacking via forged redirect messages. 2. It should only be temporarily set to 1 in controlled experimental or specialized network debugging environments, and must be reverted to 0 afterward

net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects.desc: 1. This kernel parameter controls whether IPv6 redirect messages are accepted for the default network interface. Compared to net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects, this setting applies specifically to newly created interfaces. The recommended value is 0 to enhance system security. 2. It should only be temporarily set to 1 in controlled experimental or specialized network debugging environments, and must be reverted to 0 afterward

net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range.desc: 1. This kernel parameter defines the range of local ephemeral ports available for outgoing connections, formatted as 'start_port end_port'. The recommended value is '30000 65500' to support high-concurrency connection scenarios. 2. If encountering 'Cannot assign requested address' or port exhaustion issues, the range can be expanded, but the start port must be no lower than 1024 and the end port no higher than 65535

net.ipv4.udp_rmem_min.desc: 1. This kernel parameter sets the minimum size (in bytes) of the receive buffer for each UDP socket. The kernel ensures that even if an application does not explicitly set SO_RCVBUF, the receive buffer will not fall below this value. In high-throughput or high-concurrency UDP scenarios, moderately increasing this value (e.g., to 65536) can reduce packet loss; however, it should not be set too large (e.g., over 256KB), as this may waste memory or lead to OOM conditions. The default value is typically 8192

net.ipv4.udp_wmem_min.desc: 1. This kernel parameter sets the minimum size (in bytes) of the send buffer for each UDP socket. If an application does not explicitly set the send buffer size via setsockopt(SO_SNDBUF), the kernel ensures it is at least udp_wmem_min. In high-throughput or high-concurrency UDP scenarios, moderately increasing this value (e.g., to 65536) can improve sending performance; however, setting it excessively large (e.g., 16MB) is discouraged, as it may cause excessive memory reservation and lead to memory pressure or OOM, especially with many concurrent sockets. The default value is typically 4096 or 8192
